title: Writing that flows
cando: write clear, connected emails and short essays that are easy to follow

about.text: In this lesson, you learn to write so that your reader can follow you without any effort. You listen to a colleague giving feedback on a draft email, compare two versions of a complaint letter, and write a four-paragraph opinion essay. Then you edit a real text of your own and explain your changes.
goals: Give and take feedback on a draft: It jumps from…, How about starting with…?
Link ideas with however, therefore, although and whereas, with the right punctuation.
Point back to an idea with this means that and such a.
Write a clear four-paragraph opinion essay.
Edit your own writing so it flows, and explain your changes.

chapters.title: Feedback on a draft
chapters.text:
This lesson is about writing that flows: writing that your reader can follow without any effort.
We start with feedback. Tomasz has written an email to the whole office about a move to a new building. Before he sends it, his colleague Amina reads the draft.
She is honest, but kind. First, she says what is good: the information is all there, and the tone is friendly. Then she names the problem: it's hard to follow.
Listen for two phrases. It jumps from the parking to the new desks. And: How about starting with the date of the move?
Notice that every criticism comes with a suggestion. That is what makes feedback constructive.
You also learn words for talking about writing: the structure, the wording, and the topic sentence that opens each paragraph.

chapters.title: Linking and pointing back
chapters.text:
The grammar has two parts.
The first is linking words. Although and whereas join two ideas inside one sentence. Although it's interesting, it doesn't help. The old office had parking, whereas the new one doesn't.
However and therefore are different. They start a new sentence, and they have a comma after them. The lifts will be closed. However, the stairs will be open.
So never join two full sentences with just a comma and however. That is the mistake Amina spotted.
The second part is pointing back. In the phrase this means that, the word this points back to a whole idea. And such a big change points back to something you have just described.
These small words are what hold a paragraph together.

chapters.title: One complaint, two letters
chapters.text:
Next, you read two letters about the same problem: repairs to a rented flat.
The first letter is angry and hard to follow. It jumps from the window to the light, and back to the window. It never says what the writer wants.
The second letter says what he wants at the start: a date for each repair. Then it takes the problems one by one. It even accepts that one visit failed because he was out.
Notice the small words in the second letter: Firstly, Secondly, However, Therefore. They show the reader the shape of the letter from the start.
Which letter would you answer first?
Then you write an opinion essay in four paragraphs: your opinion, your main reason with an example, the other side, and your conclusion.

chapters.title: Make it flow
chapters.text:
In the task, you work on a real text of your own. It could be an email, a report, or the essay you have just written.
Edit it so it flows. Put the ideas in a clear order. Start each paragraph with a topic sentence. Link the ideas, and check the punctuation.
Then explain three changes to a partner. Say what you changed, and why. For example: In my first version, it jumped from the kitchen to the car park. Or: I cut out this sentence, because it didn't help the reader.
Your partner may ask: Why did you move that paragraph? Answer with a reason: Because the reader needs the date first.

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a longer text. This time, read it as a writer as well as a reader.
How does the writer move from one idea to the next? Which words link the paragraphs?
Good writers use the same tools you practised in this lesson: a clear order, linking words, and words that point back.
Find one part that flows well, and one part you would tighten up. Then talk or write about it.

warmup.prompt: A colleague asks you to read their draft before they send it. What do you usually do?
choices: say it's fine, to be kind
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. Many people find it hard to comment on someone else's writing. In this lesson, you learn to do it honestly and kindly.

conversation.title: Before you press Send
conversation.setting: Tomasz has written an email to everyone in the office about next month's move to a new building. Before he sends it, he asks his colleague Amina to read the draft.
lines: Have you had a chance to look at my draft? I'd rather hear about the problems from you than from forty people.
I have. The information's all there, and the tone is friendly. But it's quite hard to follow in places.
Well, it jumps from the parking to the new desks, and then back to the parking. The structure isn't very logical.
That's fair. I didn't write an outline first. I just wrote things down in the order I thought of them.
How about starting with the date of the move? People need that first, whereas the parking can wait until the end.
That makes sense. And what about the paragraph on the history of the building?
Honestly, I'd cut it out. Although it's interesting, it doesn't help anyone pack a box.
Some of the wording is repetitive. You say ‘please note’ five times. This means that after a while, nobody notices it.
Ouch. OK, I'll tighten that up.
One last thing. You wrote: ‘The lifts will be closed, however the stairs will be open.’ However can't join two sentences with just a comma.
I'd never have spotted that. Thanks, this is really constructive. Forty people are moving on one day, so I want to get it right.
Exactly. Such a big change needs an email that everyone can follow. Send me the new version, and I'll have another look.

questions.q: What is Amina's main problem with the draft?
questions.why: Amina says the information is all there and the tone is friendly, but it's hard to follow in places.

questions.q: What does Amina suggest putting first?
questions.why: She says: How about starting with the date of the move?

questions.q: Why does Amina want to cut the paragraph about the building's history?
questions.a: It doesn't help people with the move.
wrong: It has several mistakes in it.
questions.why: She says: Although it's interesting, it doesn't help anyone pack a box.

phrases.text: Have you had a chance to look at my draft?
phrases.use: Asking a colleague politely for feedback.

phrases.text: It's quite hard to follow in places.

phrases.use: Saying the ideas are in a confusing order.
Suggesting a better way to begin.
Suggesting that a part is removed.
Promising to make a part shorter and clearer.

items.meaning: An early version of a piece of writing, which you will change before it is finished.
items.example: Can you read my draft before I send it?

items.meaning: Comments about how good or useful something is, and how to improve it.
items.example: My manager gave me some useful feedback on the report.

items.meaning: Helpful, because it shows you how to improve.
items.example: Thanks for the constructive comments.

items.meaning: Comments that say what is wrong with something or someone.
items.example: She doesn't take criticism very well.

items.meaning: The way the parts of something are arranged and connected.
items.example: The report has a clear structure: the problem, the causes, then the solutions.

items.meaning: A short plan of the main points, written before you start.
items.example: Write a quick outline before you start the essay.

items.meaning: The sentence, usually the first one, that says what a paragraph is about.
items.example: Each paragraph should start with a clear topic sentence.

items.meaning: The words that someone chooses to say or write something.
items.example: The idea is good, but the wording could be clearer.

items.meaning: The quality of being clear and easy to understand.
items.example: I rewrote the email for clarity.

items.meaning: In an order, or following reasons, that make sense.
items.example: Put the steps in a logical order.

items.meaning: Saying or doing the same thing too many times, so that it becomes boring.
items.example: The last paragraph is a bit repetitive.

items.meaning: To be clear and easy to understand; or to be a sensible thing to do.
items.example: Does this sentence make sense to you?

items.meaning: To notice something, especially something that is hard to see.
items.example: Can you spot the mistake in this sentence?

items.meaning: To remove a part from a text or a plan.
items.example: I cut out the second paragraph because it said the same thing again.

items.meaning: To make something, such as a piece of writing or a rule, shorter, clearer or stricter.
items.example: Try to tighten up your introduction.

sound.title: The pause before however
sound.explain: But and however mean almost the same, but they sound different. A joining word like but or so keeps the sentence going, so the voice runs on with only a tiny break. However and therefore start a new sentence, so there is a real pause before them, and a short one after. Listen to each pair, then say them.
lines: The lifts will be closed, but the stairs will be open.
The lifts will be closed. However, the stairs will be open.
The move is on Friday, so please pack on Thursday.
The move is on Friday. Therefore, please pack on Thursday.

sayIt.instructions: Say Amina's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Does your feedback sound helpful and kind, not rude?
lines: Well, it jumps from the parking to the new desks, and then back to the parking. The structure isn't very logical.
How about starting with the date of the move? People need that first, whereas the parking can wait until the end.
Honestly, I'd cut it out. Although it's interesting, it doesn't help anyone pack a box.
Exactly. Such a big change needs an email that everyone can follow. Send me the new version, and I'll have another look.

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the conversation. Two join ideas inside one sentence, and one joins them wrongly. Two point back to something that was said before.
examples: People need that first, whereas the parking can wait until the end.
Although it's interesting, it doesn't help anyone pack a box.
The lifts will be closed, however the stairs will be open.
This means that after a while, nobody notices it.
Such a big change needs an email that everyone can follow.
spot.question: Which words join two ideas inside one sentence? Which sentence is punctuated wrongly, and why? What do ‘This’ and ‘Such a big change’ point back to?
spot.answer: ‘Whereas’ and ‘although’ join two ideas inside one sentence, with a comma. ‘However’ cannot do that: it needs a full stop before it, so Tomasz's sentence is wrong. ‘This’ points back to the whole idea before it: saying ‘please note’ five times. ‘Such a big change’ points back to what Tomasz has just said: forty people moving on one day.

rules.title: Linking ideas: however, therefore, although, whereas
rule: although and whereas join two ideas in one sentence: Although it's long, it's clear.
whereas compares two different facts: The old office had parking, whereas the new one doesn't.
however and therefore start a new sentence, with a comma after: It's clear. However, it's long.
however means but; therefore means so, or as a result.
A test: if both halves are full sentences, a comma before however is not enough.
rules.mistake: Not: It's clear, however it's long. Say: It's clear. However, it's long.

rules.title: Pointing back: this means that, such a …
rule: this or that can point back to a whole idea: The move is on Friday. This means that…
Useful frames: This means that … This is why … That is the reason …
such a + adjective + noun points back to something described: Such a big change needs a clear plan.
With a plural or uncountable noun, use such with no a: such changes, such advice.
If this alone could be unclear, add a noun: this delay, this change.
rules.mistake: Not: A such change needs time. Say: Such a change needs time.

practice.q: The old office had a car park, ___ the new one has none.
practice.why: whereas compares two different facts inside one sentence.

practice.q: The report was late. ___, we missed the deadline.
practice.why: Therefore means as a result, and it starts a new sentence.

practice.q: ___ the email was long, everyone read it to the end.
practice.why: Although joins two ideas in one sentence: it was long, but they read it.

practice.q: The price is good. ___, the delivery is slow.
practice.why: However starts a new sentence and shows a contrast.

options: It was expensive, however we bought it.
It was expensive. However, we bought it.
It was expensive however, we bought it.
practice.a: It was expensive. However, we bought it.
practice.why: However needs a full stop before it and a comma after it.

practice.q: We are moving on Friday. ___ means that the office will be closed.
practice.why: This points back to the whole idea before it.

practice.q: Forty people are moving in one day. ___ a big change needs careful planning.
practice.why: such a + adjective + noun points back to what was just described.

practice.q: Three customers said our staff were rude. We don't often get ___ complaints.
practice.why: With a plural noun, use such with no a.

practice.q: ___ the first letter was ignored, the second was answered within a week.
practice.why: Whereas compares two different facts inside one sentence.

practice.q: Sales fell in March. This ___ that we need a new plan.
practice.why: This is singular, so this means that…

yourTurn.prompt: Write a short email of five or six sentences to your team about a change at work: new opening hours, a new system or an office move. Use at least three of these: however, therefore, although, whereas, this means that, such a.
yourTurn.model: From Monday, the office will open at 7.30 instead of 8.00. This means that the early shift can finish at 3.30. Although some of you asked for later hours, we can't offer them yet. The morning team will use the main entrance, whereas the afternoon team can use the side door. Such a change can take a few weeks to get used to. However, we will look at it again at the end of the month.

text.title: One complaint, two letters
text.type: Letter of complaint: the first draft and the letter that was sent
text.body:
PRACTICE TEXT: these people and this company are invented.

Rafael Balewa rents a flat from Ashgrove Housing. He wrote the first letter when he was angry. Then he rewrote it before he sent it.
---
VERSION 1: THE FIRST DRAFT
Dear Sir or Madam,
I am writing again about my flat because nothing has been done and I am extremely unhappy. The bathroom window has not closed since January, I reported it twice, nobody came. Also the light on the stairs is broken, it has been broken since December and it is dangerous at night. The boiler was serviced but I never got the certificate, however my insurance company needs it. I also never got the second key for the new lock, which is ridiculous. The window is the worst thing because the bathroom is freezing. Such a situation is completely unacceptable. I have kept copies of everything and I will take this further if I have to.
Yours faithfully,
Rafael Balewa
---
VERSION 2: THE LETTER HE SENT
Dear Ms Adeyemi,
Repairs still waiting: Flat 14, Priory Court
I am writing about four repairs that have still not been done. I would be grateful for a date for each one by 30 March.
Firstly, the bathroom window has not closed since 3 January. I reported it on 3 and 17 January. Secondly, the light on the second-floor landing has not worked since December. Thirdly, the boiler was serviced in November, but I have not received the safety certificate. Lastly, the front door lock was replaced, but I was given only one key.
I accept that the visit on 9 February could not go ahead because I was not at home. However, three of these four repairs do not need anyone to come into the flat.
The certificate is the most urgent, as my home insurance must be renewed in April. Therefore, I would ask you to deal with it first.
I would much rather sort this out directly with you. Nevertheless, I have kept copies of all my reports.
Yours sincerely,
Rafael Balewa

gist.q: What is the main difference between the two letters?
gist.a: Version 2 is organised and says clearly what Rafael wants.
gist.why: Both letters are about the same four repairs, but only Version 2 takes them in order and asks for something specific.

gist.q: Which letter is more likely to get a quick answer?
wrong: Neither: they say the same thing
gist.why: Version 2 asks for a date by 30 March, so the reader knows exactly what to do.

detail.q: What does Rafael ask for in Version 2?
detail.a: a date for each repair by 30 March
detail.why: He writes: I would be grateful for a date for each one by 30 March.

detail.q: What does Rafael accept in Version 2?
detail.a: One visit could not happen because he was out.
wrong: He reported the window too late.
detail.why: He accepts that the visit on 9 February could not go ahead because he was not at home.

detail.q: Why does he want the certificate first?
detail.a: His home insurance must be renewed in April.
detail.why: He writes that the certificate is the most urgent, as his home insurance must be renewed in April.

detail.q: Version 1 says: ‘I reported it twice, nobody came.’ What is wrong with the punctuation?
detail.a: A comma cannot join two full sentences.
detail.why: Both halves are full sentences, so it needs a full stop, or a joining word such as but.

items.meaning: Good at making people agree with you or do what you ask.
items.example: She wrote a persuasive letter, and the council changed its mind.

items.meaning: To give reasons why you think something is true or right.
items.example: The writer argues that city centres should be free of cars.

items.meaning: To show that something is especially important.
items.example: I want to emphasise that the deadline is Friday.

items.meaning: To make a point clearer by giving an example.
items.example: Let me illustrate the problem with a real case.

items.meaning: To make an idea or a feeling stronger, for example by adding more evidence.
items.example: The figures reinforce what customers have been telling us.

items.meaning: To make something stronger or more effective.
items.example: A clear example would strengthen your argument.

items.meaning: To make something less strong or less effective.
items.example: Too many small points can weaken a good essay.

items.meaning: To connect two things or ideas.
items.example: Use however and therefore to link your ideas.

items.meaning: Marks such as full stops, commas and question marks that divide writing into sentences and parts.
items.example: Check your punctuation before you send the email.

items.meaning: The mark (,) that separates parts of a sentence.
items.example: Put a comma after However at the start of a sentence.

model.title: A four-paragraph opinion essay
model.body:
Should buses be free?
Many towns are now asking whether buses should be free for everyone. In my opinion, they should, at least in town centres, and I would argue that the benefits are far greater than the costs.
The main benefit is less traffic. At the moment, buses sit in the same traffic jams as cars, and this means that they are slow as well as expensive. If buses were free, many drivers would leave their cars at home, so both problems would improve. Kelmouth, a town that tried free buses for a year, illustrates this well: passenger numbers rose by a third.
Of course, some people argue that free buses cost too much. Someone has to pay for the drivers and the fuel, and in the end that is the taxpayer. However, cars also cost a town money, through road repairs, accidents and poor air quality. Such costs are easy to forget, because nobody ever sends a bill for them.
In conclusion, free buses are not a perfect answer, but they are a sensible one. Although they would cost money, they would make our towns cleaner and easier to move around. Therefore, I believe more towns should try them.

write.task: Write a four-paragraph opinion essay of 200 to 250 words. Choose one question: Should shops be open on Sundays? Is it better to rent a home or to buy one? Should tourists pay extra to visit popular cities? Paragraph 1: your opinion. Paragraph 2: your main reason, with an example. Paragraph 3: the other side, and your answer to it. Paragraph 4: your conclusion.
checklist: Each paragraph starts with a clear topic sentence.
I linked ideas with however, therefore, although or whereas, and punctuated them correctly.
I pointed back at least once with this means that, this + a noun, or such a.
Paragraph 3 answers the other side, and paragraph 4 adds no new ideas.

card.title: Make it flow
card.situation: Choose a real text you have written in English: an email, a message, a short report, or your essay from Section 3. It says what you want, but it may not be easy to follow.
card.goal: Edit it so that it flows: a clear order, a topic sentence for each paragraph, good linking words and correct punctuation. Then explain three of your changes, and why you made them.

phrases: In my first version, it jumped from … to …
I moved … to the beginning, because …
I cut out … because it didn't help the reader.
I joined these two sentences with whereas.
I changed the comma to a full stop, because however starts a new sentence.
This means that the reader can …
prepare.notes: Put your first version and your new version side by side. Mark three changes. For each one, write one sentence: what you changed, and why.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, show your two versions to a partner and explain three changes. Your partner asks one question about each change. Then your teacher gives you feedback on one paragraph.
doIt.wehel: I am going to paste two versions of a text I wrote. You are my colleague. Ask me to explain three changes I made, and why I made them. Then give me constructive feedback: one thing that is better now, and one thing I could still tighten up. Use clear, simple English.

model.title: Explaining the changes
lines: Quite a lot. It's an email to our cleaning company about the new timetable. In my first version, it jumped from the kitchen to the car park and then back to the kitchen.
Now it starts with what I want: the new times, from 1 May. Then there's one paragraph for each area, and each one starts with a topic sentence.
I cut out two sentences about last year's problems. They were true, but they didn't help the reader.
I'd written: ‘The kitchen is fine, however the windows are dirty.’ I changed the comma to a full stop, because however starts a new sentence.
Yes. I said ‘the problem’ three times in one paragraph. Now the second one is ‘this delay’, so the reader knows exactly which problem I mean.
Nice. If I were them, I'd know exactly what to do.
That's the idea. Thanks for reading it.
compare: Did you explain what you changed, and why?
Did you talk about the order of your ideas, not just single words?
Did you explain at least one change to linking or punctuation?
Did you use phrases like It jumped from … and I cut out …?

canDo: I can give and take constructive feedback on a draft.
I can link ideas with however, therefore, although and whereas, and punctuate them correctly.
I can point back to an idea with this means that and such a.
I can write a clear four-paragraph opinion essay.
I can edit my own writing so it flows, and explain my changes.

reading.before: Look at the title and the first paragraph. What is the writer trying to do: tell a story, explain something, or persuade you?
reading.talk: Was the writing easy to follow? Find one place where the writer links two ideas well, and one place you would tighten up. Write three or four sentences, or discuss it with Wehel.

quiz.q: It's a good draft, but it ___ from the prices to the staff and back again.
quiz.why: It jumps from … to … means the ideas are in a confusing order.

quiz.q: Our old supplier was cheap, ___ the new one is reliable.
quiz.why: whereas compares two different facts inside one sentence.

options: The room was booked. However, nobody came.
The room was booked, however nobody came.
The room was booked however, nobody came.
quiz.a: The room was booked. However, nobody came.
quiz.why: However needs a full stop before it and a comma after it.

quiz.q: Feedback that helps you to improve is ___ .
quiz.why: Constructive feedback shows you how to improve.

quiz.q: This paragraph says the same thing three times. It's ___ .
quiz.why: Repetitive means saying the same thing too many times.

quiz.q: The first sentence of a paragraph, which says what it is about, is the ___ sentence.
quiz.why: The topic sentence tells the reader what the paragraph is about.

quiz.q: The bus fare went up by 40%. ___ a big rise was always going to cause complaints.
quiz.why: such a + adjective + noun points back to what was just described.

quiz.q: The company ___ to be in serious trouble.
quiz.why: Reporting with the passive: be said + to + verb.
fell from one figure to the new figure.

quiz.q: Prices are likely ___ again next year.
quiz.why: be likely + to + verb: what will probably happen.

liveClass: Day 1: hand out a short, badly ordered email. Pairs give feedback with It jumps from…, How about starting with…? and I'd cut out…, then rewrite the first paragraph together. Finish with the but and however pairs from the sound step.
Day 2: the task. Each learner shows the first and new versions of a real text and explains three changes; the partner asks one question about each. Then give each learner feedback on one paragraph.
Day 3: talk about the book: find one passage that flows well and one that could be tightened up. Then two learners read an essay paragraph aloud, and the class names its topic sentence.
